title: 10 BÀI ĐỌC HIỂU TIẾNG ANH – LEVEL B1+ / B2

passages.title: Reading 1 – AN INTERNATIONAL FAMILY
passages.text: Minh comes from Ho Chi Minh City, but his life is no longer centered in Vietnam. He is married to Jane, an American woman from Boston, and the couple now lives and works in France. Although Jane’s family remains in Boston, she has built a new life with Minh in Europe. Their family uses three languages—English, French, and Vietnamese—which allows them to communicate across different cultural settings.Their two children, Rose and Jack, attend a local primary school. The school is particularly international because children from many countries study there. Rose has friends from France, Switzerland, and Austria, while Jack studies with children from South Africa, Spain, and Canada. For the children, meeting classmates from different backgrounds is not unusual; it is simply part of everyday school life.The family’s situation shows that nationality does not necessarily determine where people live, work, or build relationships. Instead, modern families can connect several countries and languages at the same time.

passages.title: Reading 2 – A BALANCED WEEKEND
passages.text: Mai’s weekends are not completely free, even though she has more time than she does on weekdays. On Saturday morning, she often goes shopping with her mother at a shopping centre. Because her mother is busy during the week, this activity is also an opportunity for them to spend time together. After lunch, Mai usually downloads music and listens to hip-hop.Later in the day, she meets her friends at a youth club. They do not simply sit and talk; they exchange ideas about music and football and sometimes play games together. Mai enjoys these meetings because they allow her to relax while maintaining her friendships.Hoa has a rather different routine. Her family often goes to their second house in a small village about an hour from Ho Chi Minh City. Her grandmother and several relatives live there. Hoa can play tennis, walk with her grandmother, or simply enjoy the garden. On some Saturdays, however, she stays in the city, gets up late, does homework, and watches a football match. Although Mai and Hoa spend their free time differently, both routines combine recreation with relationships and personal responsibilities.

passages.title: Reading 3 – FINDING YOUR WAY AROUND A CITY
passages.text: A visitor who arrives in Da Nang can find many different ways to spend a weekend. The city offers well-known places such as Dragon Bridge, My Khe Beach, and Ngu Hanh Son. Dragon Bridge is especially attractive at night, when visitors can enjoy its appearance from different viewpoints.Shopping is another convenient activity. Department stores, supermarkets, and shopping centres give visitors a wide range of choices, so people can shop without travelling far from the main areas of the city. Those who prefer outdoor activities can play golf or tennis, cycle through the streets, or walk around and observe the city.Food is also an important part of the experience. Visitors can find fresh seafood in restaurants as well as a variety of coffee shops. The passage also emphasizes the character of local people, describing them as honest, friendly, and willing to help. Therefore, the city is presented not only as a place with attractive locations but also as a place where visitors can enjoy everyday services and human interaction.

passages.title: Reading 4 – MAKING HEALTHIER CHOICES
passages.text: Susan enjoys fast food, especially fried chicken and potato chips. When Frank sees what she is eating, he warns her that eating too much fast food is bad for her health. Susan explains that she is hungry, but Frank suggests choosing healthier food instead of simply eating more.He recommends fish and vegetables and advises her not to drink too much coke because it may contribute to weight gain. When Susan asks what she should drink, Frank suggests mineral water, lemon juice, or orange juice. His advice is not about avoiding food altogether; rather, it is about replacing less healthy choices with better ones.The conversation illustrates how “should” and “shouldn’t” can be used to give advice. More importantly, it shows that healthy habits often depend on everyday decisions. A small change in what someone eats or drinks can be a practical first step toward a healthier routine.

passages.title: Reading 5 – WHAT HAPPENS AT THE MOMENT?
passages.text: People often use the present simple and present continuous to describe different kinds of situations. The present simple is useful for habits and facts, while the present continuous focuses on actions happening now or around the present time.Consider a student named Alex. He usually studies English in the evening and often plays football with his friends at weekends. These are regular activities. However, today is different. He is sitting in the classroom, listening to his teacher, and writing notes. His classmates are working on an exercise, and the teacher is explaining a new activity.The contrast is important. Alex’s usual routine has not disappeared, but the writer is focusing on what is happening at this particular moment. Words such as “usually” and “often” help identify regular actions, whereas “today,” “now,” and “at the moment” signal an action in progress.

passages.title: Reading 6 – HALLOWEEN: MORE THAN A COSTUME
passages.text: Halloween is presented as a festival involving much more than wearing unusual clothes. In the United States, people may attend fancy-dress parties whose themes include horror and superpowers. Restaurants and clubs may organize special events, prepare food and drinks, and invite live bands to perform.Children have a different but equally recognizable tradition. They go from door to door, say “trick or treat,” and ask neighbours for sweets and chocolates. Another familiar activity is making lanterns with candles. People may also play games connected with the occasion.The festival therefore combines entertainment, social interaction, food, music, and traditional activities. Although costumes are one visible feature, the wider celebration involves both children and adults in different ways. The holiday also has a connection with the traditional harvest, which gives it a cultural background beyond parties and games.

passages.title: Reading 7 – TET AND FAMILY CONNECTIONS
passages.text: Tet is Vietnam’s main holiday and is described as a meaningful occasion for families to reunite. Before Tet, people often buy new clothes, clean their houses, prepare traditional foods such as banh chung and mut, and decorate their homes with flowers and plants. These preparations are practical, but they also contribute to the atmosphere of the celebration.During the holiday, people visit relatives and friends to wish them a happy New Year. Children receive lucky money from adults, while many families visit pagodas. Young people may spend time with friends by hanging out or going to amusement parks. People are also expected to behave politely toward one another.Tet therefore combines family traditions, social visits, food, religious or cultural activities, and leisure. Its importance is not limited to a single event; rather, the holiday brings several aspects of community and family life together.

passages.title: Reading 8 – A DAY IN THE CITY
passages.text: Imagine arriving in a new neighbourhood and needing to find several places. A useful way to navigate is to identify landmarks and understand basic direction phrases. A supermarket, for example, may be near a post office, while another building may be opposite it. A person giving directions can also use expressions such as “go along,” “go past,” “turn left,” or “turn right.”These expressions are useful because simply naming a destination may not tell a visitor how to reach it. Clear directions connect the starting point with the destination. For someone who is unfamiliar with the area, the difference between “near” and “opposite,” or between “turn left” and “turn right,” can completely change the route.Knowing the names of places is therefore only the first step. Effective communication also requires understanding relationships between places and the sequence of actions needed to reach a destination.

passages.title: Reading 9 – FOOD, QUANTITY AND CHOICE
passages.text: When people shop for food, they need to distinguish between items that can be counted individually and substances that are treated as uncountable. A shopper can ask how many apples or eggs are needed, but the appropriate question for milk, tea, or butter is how much. This distinction becomes especially useful when preparing a shopping list.Imagine a customer buying bread, eggs, milk, butter, apples, cookies, potatoes, carrots, strawberries, tomatoes, apple juice, cakes, cheese, and tea. Some items are naturally discussed as individual units, while others are normally measured by amount or quantity. Choosing the correct question helps the shopper communicate precisely.The same attention to choice appears in health advice. Instead of simply asking whether a food is popular, people can consider whether their diet contains a reasonable balance. Advice using “should” and “shouldn’t” can encourage healthier choices, such as eating more vegetables and drinking water rather than consuming too much fast food or soft drink.

passages.title: Reading 10 – LEISURE, ABILITY AND PERSONAL ROUTINES
passages.text: Free time can reveal a great deal about people’s interests, abilities, and routines. Some activities are usually described with “play,” such as football, badminton, tennis, or volleyball. Other activities commonly follow “go,” especially activities ending in -ing, such as swimming, jogging, or cycling. People may also “do” activities such as yoga, aerobics, or karate.Frequency adverbs add another layer of information. Someone may always play football on Sundays, often go jogging, sometimes watch films, or hardly ever play video games. These expressions help listeners understand not only what a person does but also how regularly the activity occurs.Ability is different again. The verb “can” describes what someone is able to do, while “can’t” describes a limitation. A person might love swimming but can’t swim well, or enjoy watching football even if they cannot play it. In this way, a person’s leisure profile may include preferences, frequency, and ability at the same time.

options.label: D
